title: Cuba’s Debate Is Missing What Cubans Want
gist: Orlando J. Pérez uses the summer 2026 LAPOP AmericasBarometer survey of 1,095 internet-connected Cubans to argue that both Washington and Havana are arguing about the wrong Cuba. Respondents put economic recovery and restoring the power grid ahead of political opening and sovereignty, and a plurality believe the Castro family, not formal institutions, holds power. That makes UN votes, embargoes and calls for elections poor tools for reaching the real center of power.

themes.theme: US-Cuba diplomatic escalation at the UN

insights.claim: At the UN General Assembly, Trump called Cuba a failed state whose system will fall. Hours later, on September 23, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is open to discussing a transition to new leadership and ending the embargo. Trump later said the two countries would reach a deal and doubted military action would be needed.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Washington is pairing maximum pressure with an offer to lift the embargo in exchange for a leadership transition. That creates a real, if unspecified, path to a negotiated change in Cuba's status.

insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Both sides say they are open to a deal but have defined no terms, so headline risk is high and any opening on embargo or investment is still speculative.

insights.claim: Cuba is losing diplomatic support in the hemisphere. Ecuador moved to sever ties and Costa Rica closed its embassy in March, and Cuba's July procedural motion to reopen the embargo debate passed only 136 to 9 with 30 abstentions, down from 165 votes for a more substantive resolution the previous October.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Havana is becoming more isolated as right-leaning Latin American governments line up with the U.S., which raises pressure on the regime and lowers the regional diplomatic cost of U.S. escalation.
insights.quote: This showed that Cuba had lost support since last October, when a more substantive resolution earned 165 votes.

insights.claim: The UN has called for an end to the embargo every year since 1992. Support fell from 187-2 in 2024 to 165-7 last October, and the coming vote will be a better measure of Cuba's backing. The State Department is weighing strict controls on the Cuban officials attending.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Watch the upcoming vote count. Further erosion would show Cuba's international cover weakening and might embolden U.S. pressure.

insights.claim: Cuba is going through its biggest economic crisis since independence, with crippling fuel shortages on top of a historic collapse of already derelict public infrastructure.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: The depth of the crisis raises the odds of regime instability or a forced deal, with knock-on effects for migration flows and the Caribbean energy trade.

insights.claim: In the month before the survey, 86% of respondents lost electricity every day, and Cuba's national grid collapsed again on September 18.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Grid failure is the binding constraint on daily life. Any settlement that restores fuel supply and power would carry outsized political weight with Cubans.

themes.theme: What Cubans want: economy before politics

insights.claim: In Vanderbilt LAPOP's 2026 AmericasBarometer survey of 1,095 internet-connected Cubans, three in four respondents blame their own government for the crisis. The sample is not nationally representative and skews younger and more urban, but it is the most systematic record of Cuban opinion in decades.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: This is rare quantitative evidence on Cuban sentiment, and it shows the regime's domestic legitimacy is badly eroded, at least among connected citizens.
insights.quote: Three in four respondents blame their own government for the island’s ongoing crisis.

insights.claim: Asked about Cuba's institutional future, 34% of surveyed Cubans chose an independent republic, 30% a Puerto Rico-like status and 29% annexation. 73% preferred economic development with foreign involvement over national independence without it.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Cubans are strongly open to foreign involvement, which suggests a post-transition Cuba would be receptive to foreign capital and possibly U.S. integration.
insights.quote: 34% chose an independent republic, 30% a status like Puerto Rico’s, and 29% annexation

insights.claim: A Cuban state that has based its legitimacy on defending the nation against Washington seems to have lost a large share of its citizens on that issue.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: The regime's core nationalist narrative is losing force at home, weakening its ability to rally people against U.S. pressure.
insights.quote: A state that has rested its legitimacy on defending the nation against Washington seems to have lost a large share of its citizens on that issue.

insights.claim: 77% of surveyed Cubans want economic changes as soon as possible rather than fixing institutions first, and 69% prefer economic recovery over a political opening. Two-thirds of those who blame Havana for the crisis still want recovery first.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Rubio's leadership-transition condition is respondents' second priority. A deal that delivers material relief may matter more to Cubans than immediate democratization.

themes.theme: Who really holds power in Cuba

insights.claim: Asked who makes the most important decisions in Cuba, 46% of respondents named the Castro family, about one in six the Communist Party, and 14% President Miguel Díaz-Canel. 31% said firms and people tied to the state benefit from government economic measures, versus 4% who said ordinary Cubans.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Formal office-holders are seen as secondary. Negotiations or sanctions aimed at the official government may miss the family and state-linked business network that controls power and economic rents.
insights.quote: Asked who makes the most important decisions in Cuba today, 46% named the Castro family.
insights.locator: The finding with the largest consequences

insights.claim: Cubans' perceptions match what Juan Linz and Alfred Stepan called 'sultanistic rule', where power runs through a ruling family and its clients more than through formal institutions. The fit is partial, because Cuba's party and armed forces are stronger than in the classic cases.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Transition analysis should model Cuba as a family-and-clients system, not a standard one-party state, which changes how transition paths are likely to unfold.
insights.quote: power runs through a ruling family and its clients more than through the institutions that formally hold it

insights.claim: Recognition, rupture and embargo votes are built for dealing with governments and reach the Castros only indirectly. Raúl Castro is 95, and if respondents are right, his death would leave both the family and the state-linked firms in place.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Do not assume that Raúl Castro's death triggers a transition. The family and state-linked business network could outlast him, so markets should not price a quick opening on succession alone.
insights.quote: Recognition, rupture and embargo votes are built for dealing with governments, and they reach the Castros only indirectly.
insights.locator: Washington and its partners demand elections

insights.claim: Both camps at the UN are arguing about the wrong Cuba. Havana's defenders protect a sovereignty that barely a third of connected Cubans would choose, and Washington's partners demand elections from a government that fewer than a third see as the real center of power, for people who want the lights back on first.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Current diplomatic strategies on both sides are poorly matched to Cuban realities. A durable settlement probably depends on restoring the economy and grid and on dealing with the informal power network.
insights.quote: The survey suggests that both camps at the UN are arguing about the wrong Cuba.
